bp: A visual perception system is asked to turn raw camera evidence into stable facts about the world: what objects are present, where they are, and whether the object seen now is the same one seen a moment ago. Object detection answers the first two questions, while tracking answers the identity-through-time question. The survey argues that these jobs are no longer cleanly separate. Real systems must handle ordinary video, 3D scenes, several camera views, language requests, unfamiliar categories, and bad conditions where evidence is partial. A closed list of known object names and a single-task pipeline are too narrow for that world. This paper serves researchers and builders by reviewing more than one hundred recent works and asking what shared pressures are moving the field toward unified, open-world, multi-task, and meaning-grounded visual systems.
wh: The hard part is that seeing an object is not one decision. A system must localize a patch of image, name or describe what it contains, decide whether the object is new or continuing from earlier frames, and sometimes reason across cameras, depth, text, and time. Each step can be uncertain. A partly hidden cyclist, a moving camera, rain, poor lighting, or an object category absent from training can make a confident box or track misleading. The field also has a measurement problem. Different datasets, task definitions, and evaluation metrics can reward different behaviors, so progress in one corner may not transfer to another. The survey treats this fragmentation as a scientific problem in its own right: when detection, tracking, 2D, 3D, multimodal fusion, and language-conditioned perception are studied apart, repeated patterns and neglected challenges become hard to see.
naive: A smart beginner would build two modules. First, run an object detector on every frame and draw boxes around known categories. Second, link boxes across adjacent frames by choosing nearby boxes with similar appearance. That can work in clean videos with familiar objects, but it breaks when the same object changes pose, disappears behind something, moves between camera views, or is described by language rather than by a fixed class label. It also treats errors as isolated: a bad detection creates a broken track, and a broken track gives no help back to detection. The survey exists because the field is moving beyond this brittle division.
ap: The central move is not a new detector but a reorganized map of the field. The survey collects recent object detection and tracking work across 2D, 3D, multi-view, multimodal, and vision-language settings, then studies the structures that recur across those settings. It asks which model families, datasets, metrics, and targeted challenges are shaping current research. From that comparison, the paper identifies several shifts: detection and tracking are converging into shared formulations, temporal modeling is increasingly handled by generative and diffusion-based methods, tracking can be conditioned on open vocabulary language, and uncertainty and multimodal fusion are becoming central in 3D and adverse environments. The practical idea is to make the field visible as one connected perception problem rather than a set of isolated score tables.
mech: The mechanism begins with a large set of recent papers, more than one hundred according to the abstract. Each paper is placed along several axes: whether it handles 2D images, 3D scenes, multiple views, video over time, multiple data types, or vision-language interaction. The survey then consolidates four kinds of evidence. First are models: what machinery papers use to turn visual input into object locations, identities, or trajectories. Second are datasets: what worlds, objects, viewpoints, and conditions researchers repeatedly train and test on. Third are evaluation protocols: what counts as success, such as accurate boxes, stable identities, or correct behavior under language-conditioned requests. Fourth are targeted challenges: open-world categories, uncertain 3D evidence, adverse environments, and temporal continuity. After organizing the papers, the survey looks for cross-task patterns. If a method used for detection also helps tracking, that suggests the boundary between the tasks is weakening. If language descriptions appear inside tracking, the output is no longer just a class id and path; it is an object tied to meaning. If metrics and datasets cluster around some settings more than others, the survey can show how measurement choices guide the field's attention.
math: The mathematical ideas underneath the survey are the ideas repeatedly appearing in the reviewed work. One is joint inference: instead of deciding location, category, and identity as separate guesses, a system can choose a set of mutually consistent answers. In everyday terms, it is like solving a puzzle where one piece constrains the next. Another is temporal modeling, which means using earlier and later frames as evidence about the present. Diffusion-based generative modeling, as named in the abstract, can be understood as starting from an uncertain or noisy guess and repeatedly refining it toward a plausible object state or trajectory. A third idea is multimodal fusion: combining signals from images, depth, multiple cameras, and language so that one weak source can be corrected by another. Open-vocabulary and language-conditioned tracking use similarity between visual evidence and word meaning, but that similarity is only useful if it preserves the distinctions the task needs. Uncertainty modeling is also central. It asks the system to represent how sure it is, not just what answer it prefers, because 3D scenes and adverse environments often make several explanations plausible. The tradeoff running through all of this is accuracy versus generality: broader perception systems can handle richer requests, but they must avoid becoming vague or overconfident.
dots: This paper connects to the conference's broader multimodal and vision-language thread because it treats perception as more than image classification. Nearby work on streaming social task detection and multimodal recommendation also faces the same basic pressure: visual data rarely arrives alone, and useful decisions often require text, time, user intent, or context. It connects to retrieval and ranking because open-vocabulary detection is partly a search problem: given a language request, choose the visual regions or tracks that best match it. It connects to uncertainty and model assessment because a perception system in 3D or bad weather must know when its evidence is weak. It also connects to systems work through the cost of unified models. Combining detection, tracking, generation, language, and multiple views may improve coherence, but it makes measurement, compute, and deployment harder.
ww: The survey's approach works because fragmentation hides repeated failure modes. If detection papers are read only as box prediction papers and tracking papers only as identity-linking papers, the reader misses that both are trying to maintain stable object beliefs under incomplete evidence. A unified view exposes when a method is really solving the same deeper problem in different clothing: preserving identity through time, grounding a word in pixels, reconciling several camera views, or deciding how much uncertainty to keep. Quantitative analysis of dataset use, metric choice, and challenge prevalence also matters because research fields learn from what they measure. If benchmarks mostly reward clean 2D closed-set detection, then open-world tracking, adverse environments, and uncertain 3D fusion may look secondary even when they are central to deployment. By lining up models, data, metrics, and challenges, the paper can explain not only what recent work does, but why the field is changing direction.
po: The payoff is a clearer field map for object detection and tracking. The paper gives researchers a way to see which ideas are converging, where language and generative temporal modeling are entering the pipeline, and which challenges remain underexplored. It also helps practitioners read benchmark claims more carefully. A system that performs well on one dataset or metric may not handle open vocabulary requests, 3D uncertainty, multiple views, or adverse conditions. The survey's main contribution is therefore organizational but practical: it shows how current perception research is moving toward broader, more semantically grounded systems.
limits: The abstract supports conclusions about research trends, not a proof that one formulation is best. A survey depends on which papers are selected, how categories are defined, and how faithfully datasets and metrics reflect real deployment. The abstract says the review covers more than one hundred representative works, but representation is still a judgment. It also names emerging trends without giving the detailed evidence in the input file. Because this is a survey, it can identify open problems and overlooked intersections, but it does not itself validate a new detector, tracker, dataset, or metric in the world.
